course.title: Film Studies: The Art of Cinema
course.description: A foundational tour of how movies make meaning, from mise-en-scene, cinematography, editing, and sound to the history and great movements of world cinema and the craft of reading a film critically. Structure and examples are informed by the 'History of film' article from Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia (CC BY-SA 4.0). Every example uses a widely known, real film.

lessons.title: The language of cinema: how to read a film
lessons.grammar_note: A useful habit: watch a two-minute clip twice, once for the story and once only for the craft. The second viewing is where film study begins.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Watch a film as something that was built, shot by shot, rather than something that simply happened in front of you. By the end of this lesson you will be able to break a scene into its basic units, name the main choices a director and crew make, and begin to say how those choices guide what you notice and feel. The goal is active reading: every frame is the result of decisions about what to include, what to leave out, and where to point your eye. Warm-up from the diagnostic: you saw that mise-en-scene means everything arranged inside the frame. Before we continue, ask yourself two things. First, what parts of a film live outside the single frame, across time, as one image gives way to the next? Second, when you remember a favorite movie moment, are you recalling what happened in the story, or how it was shown to you? Hold on to that difference, because it is the heart of film study.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Cinema has its own grammar. The smallest practical unit is the shot: a single continuous run of the camera, from the moment it starts recording to the moment it cuts. Shots combine into a scene, a stretch of action unified by place and time. Scenes combine into a sequence, a larger movement of the story with its own shape. Above all of this sits film form, the total system of choices, set against film content, the events and ideas the film is about. Two filmmakers can tell the same story and produce completely different films, because form, how something is shown, carries meaning of its own. Critics often separate four tools that shape every shot: mise-en-scene (what is arranged in the frame), cinematography (how it is photographed), editing (how shots are joined), and sound (what we hear). Reading a film means noticing these tools at work and asking why each choice was made, rather than letting them pass by invisibly.

sections.heading: Techniques & examples
sections.text: Consider the opening of Orson Welles's 'Citizen Kane' (1941). A 'No Trespassing' sign gives way to a slow series of dissolves that climb a fence and move toward a distant castle, Xanadu, with a single lit window. The window goes dark, then glows again; inside, a man drops a snow globe, whispers 'Rosebud,' and dies. Notice how little of this is told in words. The creeping camera, the gloom, the fairy-tale castle, and the fragile globe all do the work before a single line of plot is explained. This is form carrying meaning. As you read any scene, ask a short set of questions: What is placed in the frame, and what is kept out? Where does the light fall? How close is the camera, and is it still or moving? When does the film cut, and to what? What do we hear, and does it come from the world on screen? Each answer is a clue to intention.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Name the four tool categories that shape a shot. 2) What is the difference between a scene and a sequence? 3) In the 'Citizen Kane' opening, name one formal choice that creates unease before any plot is explained. 4) True or false: two films that tell the same story must feel the same. 5) What single question best separates content from form? Answers: 1) Mise-en-scene, cinematography, editing, and sound. 2) A scene is unified by one place and time, while a sequence is a larger run of connected scenes forming one movement of the story. 3) Any of: the slow dissolves, the gloomy low light, the looming castle, or the fragile snow globe. 4) False, because form shapes meaning, so the same story can feel wholly different. 5) Ask not only what happens, but how it is shown.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: watching only for plot, and treating the camera, cutting, and sound as a neutral window onto events. In film study the window is the subject. Mistake: assuming a choice is accidental; in a finished film almost everything in the frame was decided by someone, so ask what effect each choice has on you. Mistake: confusing a shot with a scene; a scene can contain many shots, or occasionally just one long take. Exit ticket: (a) Define a shot in one sentence. (b) Name the four formal tools of cinema. (c) Why can the same story produce two very different films? Answers: (a) A shot is a single uninterrupted run of the camera between two cuts. (b) Mise-en-scene, cinematography, editing, and sound. (c) Because film form, the how of showing, carries meaning of its own, so different formal choices yield different experiences.

lessons.title: Mise-en-scene: everything in the frame
lessons.grammar_note: Pause a film on a single frame and pretend it is a painting. Everything you can describe about that still image is mise-en-scene.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Read everything a director arranges inside the frame and explain how it shapes meaning. Mise-en-scene is a French phrase meaning, roughly, 'placing on stage,' and it covers setting, lighting, costume and makeup, and the staging of actors: their positions, movements, and gestures. By the end of this lesson you will be able to look at a single still image and describe the deliberate choices behind it. Warm-up from the diagnostic: you learned that editing is not part of mise-en-scene, because mise-en-scene is about what is arranged within the frame, before and during filming, not how frames are joined afterward. Keep that boundary in mind. As you practice, resist the urge to say a scene 'looks nice' and instead ask what the look is doing: where it sends your eye, what mood it builds, and what it tells you about a character or a world without a word of dialogue. The frame is a composition, and you are learning to read it.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Mise-en-scene is the art of the controlled frame. Its main elements are setting (location, sets, and props), lighting (its direction, intensity, and color), costume and makeup (which signal era, class, and personality), and staging or blocking (where figures stand and how they move in the space). A fifth element, performance, lives here too: posture, expression, and gesture. These parts work together to organize the viewer's attention. A brightly lit figure against a dark background pulls the eye instantly. A character pushed to the edge of a crowded frame can feel trapped or ignored. Depth matters as well: foreground, middle ground, and background can each carry action, letting a single image hold several layers of meaning at once. Because every object placed in shot took effort to put there, a careful viewer treats the frame as a composition, like a painting that also moves, and asks what each arrangement is meant to say.

sections.heading: Techniques & examples
sections.text: Film noir offers clear lessons. In 'Double Indemnity' (1944), hard low-key lighting throws barred shadows from window blinds across the actors, visually caging characters who are trapped by their own crimes. For staging and depth, 'Citizen Kane' again rewards study: deep-focus compositions keep foreground and far background equally sharp, so a small figure in the distance can comment on a large one up close within the same shot. For a modern, highly deliberate style, Wes Anderson's films, such as 'The Grand Budapest Hotel' (2014), use flat, symmetrical framing and bold, controlled color to make every set feel like a dollhouse, signaling a storybook world. To analyze mise-en-scene, move through the frame methodically: describe the setting, trace the light and where it falls, read the costumes, then note how the figures are placed and how the space uses depth. Finally, connect each observation to meaning: what does this arrangement make you feel or understand?

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) List the main elements of mise-en-scene. 2) In film noir, what does low-key lighting with heavy shadow tend to suggest? 3) What does deep focus allow a single shot to do? 4) Name one thing a costume can tell you about a character before they speak. 5) Why is where a figure stands in the frame meaningful? Answers: 1) Setting, lighting, costume and makeup, staging or blocking, and performance. 2) Danger, moral darkness, entrapment, or psychological tension. 3) Hold sharp action in the foreground and background at once, letting near and far elements comment on each other. 4) Their era, class, profession, wealth, or personality. 5) A figure pushed to the edge or hemmed in by the frame can read as marginal, trapped, or losing control, while a centered figure often reads as dominant or secure.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: praising a frame as beautiful without saying what the beauty does. In analysis, always link look to meaning. Mistake: folding editing or camera movement into mise-en-scene; those belong to cutting and cinematography. Mise-en-scene is what is arranged within the frame itself. Mistake: ignoring the background, where directors often hide the richest detail. Train your eye to scan the whole frame, not just the speaking face. Exit ticket: (a) Translate 'mise-en-scene' and name three of its elements. (b) What mood does barred, shadowy low-key lighting usually create? (c) Why should you always scan the background of a shot? Answers: (a) Roughly 'placing on stage'; any three of setting, lighting, costume and makeup, staging, and performance. (b) Tension, danger, entrapment, or moral darkness, as in film noir. (c) Because meaningful detail, action, and commentary are often staged in depth, behind the main figure.

lessons.title: Cinematography: shots, movement, and light
lessons.grammar_note: Shot size is about how much we see; angle is about where we see it from; movement is about whether the frame travels. Keep the three questions separate.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe how a film is photographed: the size and angle of its shots, how the camera moves, and how it is lit. Cinematography is the craft of the camera and light, led on set by the director of photography. By the end of this lesson you will be able to name common shot types, identify camera movements, and read lighting for mood. Warm-up from Checkpoint 1 ahead and the diagnostic: you will soon match a pan to a horizontal pivot and low-key lighting to film noir. Build toward that. As you watch, start narrating the camera to yourself: how far away is it, is it high or low, is it moving, and where is the light coming from. These sound like technical details, but each one is also an emotional choice. A face shot from below can feel powerful; the same face from above can feel small. The camera is never neutral; it always takes a position, both literally and in feeling, and learning to name that position is the whole skill.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Cinematographers work with a handful of core variables. Shot size describes how much we see: an extreme wide or establishing shot sets a whole location; a long shot shows a full body in its space; a medium shot frames from roughly the waist up; a close-up isolates a face or detail; an extreme close-up fills the screen with an eye or an object. Camera angle adds attitude: a low angle looks up and can lend power, a high angle looks down and can shrink a subject, and an eye-level angle feels neutral. Movement brings the frame to life: a pan pivots horizontally, a tilt pivots vertically, a dolly or tracking shot glides the whole camera through space, a crane lifts it, and a handheld camera shakes with nervous energy. Lighting sets mood through its key, fill, and backlight, ranging from bright, even high-key light to shadowed, high-contrast low-key light.

sections.heading: Techniques & examples
sections.text: Alfred Hitchcock's 'Vertigo' (1958) gives us the dolly zoom, where the camera tracks back while zooming in, or the reverse, so the background seems to stretch sickeningly while the subject stays put, a perfect image of dizziness and dread. Steven Spielberg borrows the same effect for Chief Brody's shock on the beach in 'Jaws' (1975). For movement, the long tracking shots that open Orson Welles's 'Touch of Evil' (1958) carry us unbroken through a tense border town, building suspense by refusing to cut. For angle, the low shots of Kane in 'Citizen Kane' make him loom over the frame. To read cinematography, ask three questions of any shot: how much do we see (size), from what position (angle), and is the frame still or moving, and why. Then read the light: is it bright and open, or dark and sculpted, and what feeling does that create?

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Order these from widest to tightest: close-up, establishing shot, medium shot. 2) What feeling does a low-angle shot often give its subject? 3) Name the camera movement where the whole camera glides smoothly through space. 4) What does the dolly zoom distort, and what feeling does it create? 5) What is the difference between high-key and low-key lighting? Answers: 1) Establishing shot, medium shot, close-up. 2) Power, dominance, or threat, because we look up at it. 3) A dolly or tracking shot. 4) It warps the apparent depth of the background while the subject stays fixed, creating unease, vertigo, or shock. 5) High-key lighting is bright and fairly even with soft shadows, while low-key lighting is darker and high-contrast, with deep, dramatic shadows.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: confusing a pan or tilt, where the camera pivots in place, with a dolly or tracking shot, where the whole camera moves through space. Pivot versus travel is the key difference. Mistake: confusing a zoom with a dolly; a zoom changes the lens while the camera stays put and tends to flatten space, while a dolly truly moves and preserves depth. Mistake: calling every dark scene 'low-key' when the shadows are just underexposed; low-key is a deliberate, sculpted contrast. Exit ticket: (a) From widest to tightest, order establishing shot, close-up, and long shot. (b) Does a low angle tend to empower or diminish its subject? (c) Name one film that uses the dolly zoom. Answers: (a) Establishing shot, long shot, close-up. (b) Empower it. (c) 'Vertigo' or 'Jaws.'

lessons.title: Editing: continuity and montage
lessons.grammar_note: When you notice a cut, you are usually watching montage; when you do not, you are usually watching continuity editing doing its job.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain how editing joins shots into a coherent, meaningful whole, and tell the two great traditions apart: continuity editing and montage. Editing is the stage where a film is truly assembled, and the order, rhythm, and type of cuts shape both clarity and emotion. By the end of this lesson you will be able to recognize the standard tools of invisible Hollywood cutting and the bolder, collision-based montage developed in the Soviet Union. Warm-up from the diagnostic: you learned that shot/reverse shot is the pattern that covers a conversation, and that 'Battleship Potemkin' is famous for its montage. Those two facts sit at opposite ends of editing's spectrum. One style hides its cuts to keep you absorbed in the story; the other makes its cuts felt, so that meaning springs from the collision of images. Knowing which is at work, and why, is one of the most useful skills in film study.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Continuity editing, the dominant Hollywood system, aims to make cutting invisible so the story flows smoothly. Its rules include the 180-degree rule (keeping the camera on one side of an imaginary line so screen direction stays consistent), the establishing shot (orienting us before we move closer), shot/reverse shot (alternating between two speakers), the eyeline match (cutting to what a character looks at), and the match on action (cutting during a movement so it seems continuous). Montage takes the opposite view. The Soviet filmmakers of the 1920s, above all Sergei Eisenstein, argued that meaning is created by the collision of shots: two images joined together produce an idea that neither holds alone. Lev Kuleshov had already shown, in the Kuleshov effect, that the same neutral face seems to express hunger, grief, or desire depending on the shot placed next to it. Editing, in this view, is where a film thinks.

sections.heading: Techniques & examples
sections.text: Eisenstein's 'Battleship Potemkin' (1925) contains the most studied edited sequence in cinema: the Odessa Steps. Soldiers march down a long staircase firing on fleeing civilians, and Eisenstein cuts rapidly among marching boots, terrified faces, a mother, and a baby carriage bouncing down the steps. No single shot shows the whole massacre; the horror is built by the collision and rhythm of fragments. By contrast, almost any classical Hollywood dialogue scene, such as a conversation in 'Casablanca' (1942), uses smooth shot/reverse shot cutting that you barely notice. Note also that the word montage carries a second, looser meaning in American usage: a compressed sequence, like a training montage, that shows the passage of time. To read editing, count how often a scene cuts, ask whether the cuts are hidden or emphasized, and notice what each new shot adds. Fast cutting raises tension; long takes let tension build within the frame instead.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What is the goal of continuity editing? 2) State the 180-degree rule in one sentence. 3) What does the Kuleshov effect demonstrate? 4) Which sequence in 'Battleship Potemkin' is the classic example of montage? 5) What two meanings can the word 'montage' carry? Answers: 1) To make cuts invisible so the story flows smoothly and the viewer stays absorbed. 2) Keep the camera on one side of an imaginary line through the action so that screen direction stays consistent. 3) That a shot's meaning depends on the shots around it; the same face reads differently next to different images. 4) The Odessa Steps sequence. 5) The Soviet idea of meaning through the collision of shots, and the looser American sense of a compressed, time-passing sequence.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking editing is just trimming; in fact the choice of what to cut to, and when, creates meaning that no single shot contains. Mistake: using 'montage' loosely without saying which sense you mean, the Eisenstein collision or the time-passing sequence. Name the sense you intend. Mistake: assuming faster cutting is always better; long takes can build dread or intimacy that rapid cutting would shatter, so match the rhythm to the purpose. Exit ticket: (a) Name three tools of continuity editing. (b) Who is the filmmaker most associated with montage theory, and which film shows it best? (c) In one line, what does the Kuleshov effect prove? Answers: (a) Any three of the 180-degree rule, establishing shot, shot/reverse shot, eyeline match, and match on action. (b) Sergei Eisenstein; 'Battleship Potemkin.' (c) Meaning comes from the relationship between shots, not from a shot alone.

lessons.title: Sound and music in film
lessons.grammar_note: A quick test for any sound: could a character in the scene hear it? If yes, it is diegetic; if only you can hear it, it is non-diegetic.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Listen to a film as carefully as you watch it, and name what its soundtrack is doing. A film's sound has three strands: dialogue, sound effects, and music, and each can come from within the story world or from outside it. By the end of this lesson you will be able to tell diegetic sound from non-diegetic sound, describe how music shapes emotion, and hear silence as a deliberate choice. Warm-up from the diagnostic: you learned that diegetic sound has a source in the story world, like a character's radio, while non-diegetic sound, such as a mood-setting score, does not. Hold that distinction close, because it unlocks most of sound analysis. Sound is the half of cinema we most often take for granted, yet it does enormous work: it tells us where we are, what to feel, and what to fear, often before the image makes it clear. Train your ears and a whole layer of filmmaking opens up.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Film sound divides first by type: dialogue (the words characters speak), sound effects (everything from footsteps to explosions), and music. It divides again by source. Diegetic sound comes from within the story world, so the characters could in principle hear it: a slamming door, a jukebox, a line of speech. Non-diegetic sound sits outside that world and is heard only by us, most often the musical score and voice-over narration. Filmmakers play across this line deliberately. Music can set mood, signal a genre, mark a time and place, and bind scenes together. A leitmotif, a short musical phrase tied to a character or idea, can return to remind us of that person even when they are off screen. Sound also guides attention and builds space: an off-screen noise can make us turn, or dread what we cannot see. And silence, used sparingly, can be louder than any score.

sections.heading: Techniques & examples
sections.text: John Williams's two-note theme in 'Jaws' (1975) is non-diegetic and functions as a warning: when it rises, the shark is near, even when the water looks calm. Bernard Herrmann's shrieking strings in the shower scene of 'Psycho' (1960) turn a montage of brief shots into pure terror, proving how far music drives the feeling of a sequence. A leitmotif at its most elaborate appears across John Williams's 'Star Wars' (1977) scores, where recurring themes announce characters and ideas. The coming of synchronized sound itself reshaped the art: 'The Jazz Singer' (1927) is remembered as the first feature-length film with spoken dialogue, helping to end the silent era. To analyze sound, first ask of any element whether it is diegetic or non-diegetic. Then ask what the music is doing to your emotions, whether any motif recurs, and whether a sudden silence or an off-screen sound is being used to steer your attention or your fear.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Name the three strands of film sound. 2) Define diegetic and non-diegetic sound. 3) What is a leitmotif? 4) Which 1927 film is famous as the first feature with spoken dialogue? 5) Give one effect that silence can create. Answers: 1) Dialogue, sound effects, and music. 2) Diegetic sound has a source in the story world and could be heard by the characters, while non-diegetic sound exists only for the audience, like the score or voice-over. 3) A short, recurring musical phrase tied to a particular character, place, or idea. 4) 'The Jazz Singer.' 5) Tension, dread, shock, intimacy, or emphasis, depending on how it is placed; silence after loud sound can feel especially heavy.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming all music is non-diegetic; a song playing on a character's car stereo is diegetic and can even cross the line when the score picks it up. Listen for the source. Mistake: ignoring sound effects, which quietly build realism and can be exaggerated for feeling, like footsteps that seem too loud in an empty house. Mistake: treating silence as an absence rather than a choice; filmmakers drop the sound on purpose. Exit ticket: (a) Is a character's on-screen radio diegetic or non-diegetic? (b) What is the main job of a non-diegetic score? (c) What ended the silent era around 1927? Answers: (a) Diegetic, because its source is in the story world. (b) To shape the audience's emotion and signal mood, tension, or genre from outside the story. (c) The arrival of synchronized recorded sound, marked by 'The Jazz Singer.'

lessons.title: From the Lumieres to classical Hollywood
lessons.grammar_note: Two founding impulses still split cinema today: the Lumiere urge to record the real world, and the Melies urge to invent a new one.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Place the first decades of cinema in order and explain how film grew from a fairground novelty into a global industry with its own genres. By the end of this lesson you will be able to describe the contributions of the Lumiere brothers and Georges Melies, characterize the silent era, and define the classical Hollywood studio system and the idea of genre. Warm-up from the diagnostic: you learned that the Lumiere brothers held early public screenings of short actuality films in the 1890s. That is where we begin. This history is not just names and dates; each step added a tool we still use. The Lumieres showed that a moving photograph of real life could hold an audience. Melies showed that the camera could lie beautifully, conjuring fantasy. The silent era refined visual storytelling, and Hollywood turned all of it into a repeatable, industrial art organized around stars, studios, and familiar story types.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Cinema's public birth is usually dated to 1895, when Louis and Auguste Lumiere screened short actuality films, such as workers leaving their factory, to a paying audience. Their camera recorded the real world in brief, single shots. Georges Melies, a magician, took film in the opposite direction, using trick effects and painted sets to create fantasy, most famously in 'A Trip to the Moon' (1902). Across the silent era, which ran into the late 1920s, filmmakers developed editing, camera movement, and performance into a sophisticated visual language, relying on intertitles and live music rather than recorded speech. By the 1920s and 1930s, the American studios had built the classical Hollywood system: a small number of large companies that controlled production, distribution, and exhibition, promoted stars, and worked in recognizable genres, patterns of story and style such as the Western, the musical, the gangster film, and later film noir, that set audience expectations.

sections.heading: Techniques & examples
sections.text: The Lumiere program reportedly included 'Arrival of a Train at La Ciotat' (1896); the sight of a train rushing toward the camera is the founding image of cinema's power to astonish. Melies's 'A Trip to the Moon' (1902), with its rocket lodged in the moon's eye, shows early special effects and set design in the service of pure imagination. From the silent era, the controlled comic choreography of a Charlie Chaplin or Buster Keaton film demonstrates how much could be said without a word. For the studio era and genre, 'Casablanca' (1942) shows the system's polish and star power, while John Ford's 'Stagecoach' (1939) helped define the Western and the convention-rich landscape of Monument Valley. To study this period, ask what each film made newly possible, and, for any genre film, which conventions it follows and which it bends.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) In roughly what year is cinema's first public screening usually dated? 2) What kind of films were the Lumiere brothers known for? 3) How did Melies's approach differ from the Lumieres'? 4) Name two genres of the classical Hollywood system. 5) What three things did the big studios typically control? Answers: 1) Around 1895. 2) Short actuality films showing real, everyday events in single shots. 3) Melies used trick effects, painted sets, and fantasy, treating film as magic rather than as a record of reality. 4) Any two of the Western, the musical, the gangster film, and film noir. 5) Production, distribution, and exhibition, along with the careers of their contracted stars, giving them control from filming all the way to the cinema screen.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: crediting a single person with inventing cinema; it emerged from many hands, with the Lumieres and Melies among the most important early figures pulling in different directions. Mistake: imagining silent films as primitive; by the 1920s they were a mature, expressive art. Mistake: treating genre as a rigid cage; strong genre films often work by bending or questioning their own conventions. Exit ticket: (a) Name the two early French pioneers discussed and the direction each pushed film. (b) What marked the end of the silent era? (c) Define genre in one sentence. Answers: (a) The Lumiere brothers, toward recording reality, and Georges Melies, toward fantasy and effects. (b) The arrival of synchronized sound in the late 1920s. (c) A genre is a recognizable pattern of story and style, such as the Western or musical, that shapes what an audience expects.

lessons.title: Movements: Expressionism, Neorealism, the New Wave
lessons.grammar_note: A quick memory hook: Expressionism paints a nightmare, Neorealism films the street, and the New Wave signs the director's name.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Identify three film movements that changed how movies look and think, and name a landmark film from each. A film movement is a group of filmmakers, usually bound by a time and place, who share a style and a set of ideas. By the end of this lesson you will be able to describe German Expressionism, Italian Neorealism, and the French New Wave, and say what each one reacted against. Warm-up from the diagnostic: you learned that Italian Neorealism is marked by location shooting and nonprofessional actors. Keep that as your anchor for one of the three. Movements matter because they show cinema arguing with itself. Each of these grew from a specific moment, an anxious Germany, a devastated postwar Italy, a restless young France, and each answered the question of what film should be in a strikingly different way. Learning them gives you a map of film style far beyond Hollywood.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: German Expressionism flourished in the 1910s and 1920s. Reacting against realism, it used distorted, angular sets, extreme shadows, and stylized acting to externalize inner states of fear and madness, shaping the look of horror and film noir for decades. Italian Neorealism arose in the mid-1940s, out of the ruins of the Second World War. It rejected studio polish in favor of real streets, natural light, nonprofessional actors, and simple, humane stories about ordinary people and hardship. The French New Wave broke out around 1959 and 1960. Young critics turned directors, writing for the magazine Cahiers du Cinema, championed the auteur theory, the idea that a director is the true author of a film, and then made films of their own: loose, personal, playful, shot on location with light equipment, and full of rule-breaking touches like the jump cut.

sections.heading: Techniques & examples
sections.text: German Expressionism is embodied by 'The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari' (1920), with its painted, crooked sets, and by F. W. Murnau's 'Nosferatu' (1922) and Fritz Lang's 'Metropolis' (1927). Italian Neorealism is captured in Vittorio De Sica's 'Bicycle Thieves' (1948), which follows a poor father and son searching for a stolen bicycle through real Roman streets, and in Roberto Rossellini's 'Rome, Open City' (1945). The French New Wave is defined by Jean-Luc Godard's 'Breathless' (1960), famous for its abrupt jump cuts, and Francois Truffaut's 'The 400 Blows' (1959), a personal story of a troubled boy ending on a celebrated freeze frame. To connect a movement to a film, ask what the film rejects, where and how it was shot, and what it believes film should do: record real life, stage a nightmare, or express a director's personal voice.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which movement used distorted sets and heavy shadow to show inner states? 2) What two production habits define Italian Neorealism? 3) What does the auteur theory claim? 4) Name the landmark Neorealist film about a stolen bicycle. 5) Which editing device is 'Breathless' famous for? 6) Name a film from German Expressionism. Answers: 1) German Expressionism, which arose in Germany in the 1910s and 1920s. 2) Shooting on real locations and using nonprofessional actors, with natural light and ordinary stories. 3) That the director is the true author of a film, stamping it with a personal vision. 4) 'Bicycle Thieves.' 5) The jump cut, which breaks smooth continuity on purpose. 6) 'The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari,' 'Nosferatu,' or 'Metropolis.'

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: mixing up the movements' looks; Expressionism is stylized and shadowed, while Neorealism is plain and lifelike, almost their opposite. Mistake: thinking the French New Wave invented the director; the auteur theory argued the director was the author even within the old studio system, then the New Wave put the idea into practice. Mistake: treating a jump cut as an error; in 'Breathless' it is a deliberate signature. Exit ticket: (a) Match each movement to its period: German Expressionism, Italian Neorealism, French New Wave. (b) Which movement prized nonprofessional actors and real locations? (c) What is an auteur? Answers: (a) German Expressionism, the 1910s to 1920s; Italian Neorealism, the mid-1940s; French New Wave, around 1959 to 1960. (b) Italian Neorealism. (c) A director treated as the true author of a film, whose personal style unifies the work.

lessons.title: Narrative, screenwriting, and reading a film critically
lessons.grammar_note: A good critical sentence sounds like 'The film does X by means of Y, which creates Z.' If you cannot name the Y, you are summarizing, not analyzing.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Map a film's story onto the three-act structure and write a short, evidence-based critical reading of a scene or a whole film. This final lesson brings the course together: you will use everything, mise-en-scene, cinematography, editing, sound, history, and movements, to say not just what a film does but how and why. By the end you will be able to identify a film's acts and turning points and build an argument supported by specific details. Warm-up from the diagnostic: you learned that the three-act structure divides a story into setup, confrontation, and resolution. That shape is your starting frame. Critical analysis is not about liking or disliking a film. It is about reading it closely and making a claim you can defend with evidence from the screen. The skill you practice here, observe, interpret, and support, is the heart of film study and the reason the earlier lessons matter.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Most mainstream films follow a three-act structure. Act One, the setup, introduces the world, the protagonist, and their goal, and ends with an inciting incident that sets the story in motion and a first turning point that locks the hero into the conflict. Act Two, the confrontation, develops rising action, obstacles, and stakes, often passing through a midpoint shift and a low point where all seems lost. Act Three, the resolution, drives to the climax, the story's peak of tension, and then the aftermath. Screenwriters build this spine from a protagonist with a clear want, an antagonist or opposing force, and conflict between them. Critical analysis then layers the formal tools on top: you ask how the filmmaking, its framing, light, cutting, and sound, supports or complicates the story. A strong reading makes a specific claim, a thesis, and backs it with concrete evidence you can point to on screen.

sections.heading: Techniques & examples
sections.text: George Lucas's 'Star Wars' (1977) is a clear three-act model: Act One sets up Luke on his home planet and launches him with the inciting attack and his aunt and uncle's death; Act Two develops the rescue and training with mounting danger; Act Three climaxes in the trench run on the Death Star. To analyze critically, move from observation to argument. Suppose you claim that 'Citizen Kane' presents its hero as unknowable. You would gather evidence: the fractured, multi-narrator structure, the deep-focus shots that place Kane amid things he cannot possess, and the final reveal of 'Rosebud' that the characters never learn. Each detail supports the thesis. Build your own reading the same way: state a claim in one sentence, then supply three or four concrete pieces of evidence from mise-en-scene, cinematography, editing, or sound, and explain how each one backs the claim. Avoid plot summary; interpret.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Name the three acts and the main job of each. 2) What is an inciting incident? 3) What is the climax of a story? 4) In critical analysis, what is a thesis? 5) Why is plot summary not the same as analysis? Answers: 1) Act One, the setup, introduces world, character, and goal; Act Two, the confrontation, develops conflict and obstacles; Act Three, the resolution, delivers the climax and aftermath. 2) The early event that disrupts the ordinary world and launches the main story. 3) The point of highest tension, where the central conflict comes to a head. 4) A clear, arguable claim about the film that the rest of your reading supports with evidence. 5) Summary only retells what happens, while analysis makes a claim about how and why the film works and defends it with specific evidence.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: confusing summary with analysis; retelling the plot is not an argument, so always ask 'so what?' and make a claim. Mistake: asserting a reading with no evidence; point to specific choices on screen. Mistake: forcing every film into a rigid three-act mold; the structure is a useful map, not a law, and many great films, especially from the movements you studied, bend or ignore it. Exit ticket: (a) Name the three acts in order. (b) What two things must a critical claim have to be persuasive? (c) In one sentence, how does analysis differ from summary? Answers: (a) Setup, confrontation, resolution. (b) A clear, arguable thesis and specific evidence from the film to support it. (c) Summary says what happens, while analysis argues how and why the film creates its meaning, using evidence from its form.
